runs.title: Establish the baseline: can semantic execution reduce agent work?
runs.story: Run 1 starts with the smallest useful experiment: the same customer-exposure-review business process is completed through a conventional application/tool flow and through Foundgine. The purpose is not to prove speed. It is to establish whether the semantic path can compress the agent interaction while reaching exactly the same final state.
runs.why: This is the control experiment. If the semantic boundary cannot reduce the number of application interactions or context carried between them, the later scalability and efficiency tests have little to build on.
runs.finding: The semantic flow reduced tool calls from 7 to 4 and estimated context load from 932 to 534 tokens (42.7% lower), while reaching the same final state. The trade-off was higher wall-clock time: 12.69 ms conventional versus 24.25 ms Foundgine (+91.1%). The early result therefore supports an agent-work reduction, not a latency claim.
runs.meaning: Foundgine was already changing the shape of the agent interaction before optimization: fewer application-level steps and less estimated context, but with execution overhead that later runs needed to investigate.

runs.title: Scale the agent workflow: does the reduction survive larger customer tiers?
runs.story: Run 2 moves from one deterministic customer to four workload tiers: 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 customers, combined with concurrency levels up to 64. The goal is to see whether the semantic reduction survives when the fixture and parallelism grow.
runs.why: A capability that looks efficient on a tiny fixture is not enough. Agents eventually operate against larger datasets and multiple simultaneous requests, so the benchmark needs to separate agent-work reduction from backend scaling behaviour.
runs.finding: The conventional path used 9 tool calls versus 6 for Foundgine, a one-third reduction, and estimated context load was about 26.5% lower. The published cells reported 100% request success. Latency was mixed: for example, at 10,000 customers/C64 the conventional path averaged 98.3 ms versus 131.2 ms for Foundgine. The run therefore shows that agent-work compression persisted, while execution speed remained workload-dependent.
runs.meaning: Run 2 established an important distinction: fewer agent interactions do not automatically mean lower end-to-end latency. The benchmark needs to measure both dimensions independently.

runs.title: Measure efficiency: what happens when the workflow itself becomes larger?
runs.story: Run 3 deliberately increases the amount of agent/tool work represented by the scenario. It asks whether the semantic path can reduce the amount of context and tool coordination without introducing a proportionally larger execution penalty.
runs.why: If the value of semantic execution is partly about reducing orchestration work, the effect should become visible when the workflow has more steps to coordinate. This run isolates that efficiency question from the later graph-performance benchmark.
runs.finding: The conventional flow used 56 tool calls versus 32 for Foundgine (42.9% fewer), and estimated context load fell from 7,568 to 4,364 tokens (42.3% lower). Average wall-clock time was almost flat: 14.64 ms versus 15.16 ms (+3.6%). Both flows reached the same final state.
runs.meaning: Run 3 is where the efficiency story becomes more compelling: the amount of agent-side work falls materially without the large latency penalty seen in Run 1.

runs.title: Measure graph execution at scale: can semantic traversal stay fast?
runs.story: Run 4 measures the agent-facing customer-exposure workflow across four customer tiers and four concurrency levels, comparing the conventional GraphQL + Hot Chocolate + EF Core path with MCP + Foundgine.
runs.why: Run 4 isolates graph execution performance after the earlier runs established the agent-work reduction. It asks whether semantic graph execution can scale while preserving the same customer-exposure result.
runs.finding: Across the published 4 × 4 workload/concurrency matrix, Foundgine sustained materially higher agent-flow throughput than the conventional GraphQL + Hot Chocolate + EF Core path. At 10 customers/C8, the published RPS was about 1,488 versus 302 (4.94×). The Run 4 aggregate contains 32 rows covering all 16 cells and both implementations, with the agent-only samples used for the comparison.
runs.meaning: Run 4 is the performance/scalability result for the semantic graph path. Unlike Runs 1–3, this experiment is a full workload/concurrency matrix and should be read independently from the later high-assurance mutation benchmarks.

metrics.implementations: GraphQL + Hot Chocolate + EF vs MCP + Foundgine

runs.title: Test the capability boundary: high-assurance TransferFunds through the same MCP protocol
runs.story: Run 5 asks a different architectural question. The operation is a high-assurance TransferFunds capability with tenant isolation, ownership, authorization revalidation, frozen-account checks, available-funds and daily-limit checks, idempotency, audit evidence and an atomic transaction. Both paths expose the same capability through MCP. The conventional path uses a purpose-built MCP tool backed by EF Core; the Foundgine path uses MCP + Foundgine High-Assurance Postgres. MCP is the common agent-facing protocol — the experiment changes what happens behind MCP.
runs.why: This is the test of whether semantic execution is useful beyond graph reads. The interesting comparison is not 'which endpoint is faster?' but whether an agent can consume a business capability without every capability becoming another handcrafted endpoint and orchestration contract.
runs.finding: Foundgine delivered higher logical-transfer throughput in every published Run 5 cell after applying the runner's native batch accounting. Across the 16 workload/concurrency cells it sustained about 2.02–3.87× the MCP + EF Core logical RPS (mean about 3.00×). At 10,000 customers/C64 it averaged about 3,633 logical transfers/s versus 1,638 for MCP + EF Core (2.22×). The Foundgine MCP request itself had higher wall time there (about 89.8 ms versus 33.3 ms) because one Foundgine request carries 8 logical transfers while the EF Core request carries one; raw request latency is therefore not an apples-to-apples per-transfer latency comparison. Zero failures were recorded in the published cells.
runs.meaning: Run 5 shows the important distinction between request latency and business-operation throughput. The Foundgine path batches eight TransferFunds operations into one set-based request, so a batch request can take longer while still completing substantially more logical transfers per second. The website should compare logical RPS for throughput and label raw wall time as per MCP request, not as equivalent per-transfer latency.

metrics.toolCalls: EF Core: 1 call/transfer; Foundgine: 1 call/8-transfer batch
metrics.wallC64: per MCP request: 33.3 vs 89.8 ms (1 op vs 8-op batch)

runs.title: Isolate the variable: same client, same logical task, individual calls versus one semantic batch call
runs.story: Run 5b is a controlled follow-up to Run 5. It reuses the exact Run 5 HttpClient and manual JSON-RPC MCP transport, unchanged, against both endpoints, so the client itself cannot explain any difference. The only thing that changes is the shape of the request: the conventional path sends batchSize individual transfer_funds MCP calls, while Foundgine sends one transfer_funds_batch MCP call carrying the same batchSize logical transfers. The matrix repeats the same 4 workload tiers (10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 customers) and 4 concurrency levels (8, 16, 32, 64) as Run 5, with 5 warmups and 30 measured runs per cell.
runs.why: Run 5 found that the Foundgine path hit a scalability cliff at concurrency 64. Before treating that as a property of the execution architecture, the benchmark needed to rule out a simpler explanation: an artifact of how many separate requests each path was making at the transport layer. Holding the client fixed and only changing individual-call versus batch-call shape isolates that variable directly.
runs.finding: Using the same client on both sides and reconstructing throughput with the runner's correct slowest-worker-per-iteration method, Foundgine's single semantic batch call outperformed the conventional path in every one of the 16 published cells. The corrected RPS advantage ranges from about 2.19× to 3.79× (mean 2.86×). At 10,000 customers/C64, Foundgine averaged about 3,570 logical transfers/s versus 1,582, with average task wall time 92 ms versus 308 ms. Tool calls remain 8 → 1 per task, and the published samples contain zero failures.
runs.meaning: Run 5b confirms the batch-call advantage with the client held constant, but its published RPS must be computed at the concurrent-iteration boundary rather than by averaging per-task instantaneous rates. The aggregate and matrix builders now use that same methodology, preventing optimistic throughput inflation from stragglers.
